Let $k$ be a field and let $H$ be a $k$-vector space with associative unital multiplication $m$, unit $1_H$, coassociative comultiplication $\Delta:H\to H\otimes_k H$, and counit $\varepsilon:H\to k$. Assume $\Delta$ and $\varepsilon$ are unital algebra maps; this is the bialgebra interface used on this page. A left $H$-module is a unital left module in the sense of [[def-left-and-right-modules]]: its action satisfies $1_Hv=v$ and $(hh')v=h(h'v)$. Let $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ be the category whose objects are all left $H$-modules and whose morphisms $f:V\to W$ are $k$-linear maps satisfying $f(hv)=h f(v)$ for every $h\in H$ and $v\in V$.

For left $H$-modules $V,W$, give the algebraic tensor product $V\otimes_k W$ the candidate action

$$h\cdot(v\otimes w)=\sum h_{(1)}v\otimes h_{(2)}w,\qquad \Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.$$

The sums are finite algebraic tensor sums; the tensor product and scalar conventions are those of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. The candidate unit object is $k_\varepsilon=k$ with $h\cdot c=\varepsilon(h)c$. For morphisms $f:V\to V'$ and $g:W\to W'$, the candidate tensor morphism is the usual linear map $f\otimes g$ determined by $(f\otimes g)(v\otimes w)=f(v)\otimes g(w)$ through [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]].

These formulas specify the proposed tensor operations; [[thm-hh-bialgebra-module-tensor-coherence]] proves that they are module actions and that the canonical associator and unit maps are morphisms in $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A,B$ be $R$-algebras. The $R$-module $A\otimes_RB$ has a unique $R$-algebra structure satisfying

$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$$

and

$$1_{A\otimes_RB}=1_A\otimes1_B,\qquad r\longmapsto r(1_A\otimes1_B).$$

If $A$ and $B$ are commutative, then $A\otimes_RB$ is commutative.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, $N$ a left $R$-module, and

$$\tau:M\times N\longrightarrow M\otimes_RN,\qquad \tau(m,n)=m\otimes n.$$

The map $\tau$ is balanced ([[def-balanced-and-bilinear-maps]]). For every abelian group $A$ and every balanced map $b:M\times N\to A$, there is a unique group homomorphism

$$\overline b:M\otimes_RN\longrightarrow A$$

such that $\overline b(m\otimes n)=b(m,n)$ for all $m,n$. Consequently composition with $\tau$ is a bijection

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ab}}(M\otimes_RN,A)\cong\operatorname{Bal}_R(M,N;A).$$

Let $R$ be a unital ring. For every left $R$-module $N$ and every right $R$-module $M$, the maps

$$\lambda_N:R\otimes_RN\longrightarrow N,\qquad r\otimes n\longmapsto rn,$$

and

$$\rho_M:M\otimes_RR\longrightarrow M,\qquad m\otimes r\longmapsto mr,$$

are group isomorphisms. Their inverses are $n\mapsto1_R\otimes n$ and $m\mapsto m\otimes1_R$, respectively. The maps respect every displayed outer module structure.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $L,M,N$ be $R$-modules. There are natural $R$-module isomorphisms

$$\sigma_{M,N}:M\otimes_RN\longrightarrow N\otimes_RM,\qquad \sigma_{M,N}(m\otimes n)=n\otimes m,$$

and

$$\alpha_{L,M,N}:(L\otimes_RM)\otimes_RN\longrightarrow L\otimes_R(M\otimes_RN),\qquad \alpha((l\otimes m)\otimes n)=l\otimes(m\otimes n).$$

Moreover $\sigma_{N,M}\sigma_{M,N}$ is the identity.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

1. **Naturality.** $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ are natural in all variables: for linear maps the usual squares commute; the unit isomorphisms are natural as well.
2. **Pentagon.** $(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\alpha_{M,N,X})\circ\alpha_{L,M\otimes N,X}\circ(\alpha_{L,M,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_X)=\alpha_{L,M,N\otimes X}\circ\alpha_{L\otimes M,N,X}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes X\to L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes X))$.
3. **Unit triangle.** $(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\lambda_N)\circ\alpha_{M,k,N}=\rho_M\otimes\mathrm{id}_N$ as maps $(M\otimes k)\otimes N\to M\otimes N$.
4. **First symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha_{L,N,M}\circ(\sigma_{N,L}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}=(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})\circ\alpha_{L,M,N}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\to L\otimes(N\otimes M)$.
5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

derivations.claim: For left $H$-modules $V,W$, the four-variable map $(a,b,v,w)\mapsto av\otimes bw$ is $k$-multilinear, so the tensor universal property [F4] defines an action of $H\otimes H$ on $V\otimes W$ by $(a\otimes b)(v\otimes w)=av\otimes bw$. On pure tensors, $(a\otimes b)((c\otimes d)(v\otimes w))=acv\otimes bdw=((a\otimes b)(c\otimes d))(v\otimes w)$ by [F2] and [F3], and $1_H\otimes1_H$ acts as the identity; pure tensors span, so this is a unital algebra action. Composing its representation map with the algebra map $\Delta$ gives precisely the candidate action of [F1], $h(v\otimes w)=\sum h_{(1)}v\otimes h_{(2)}w$, as a unital left $H$-module action.

If $f:V\to V'$ and $g:W\to W'$ are $H$-linear, then on each pure tensor $(f\otimes g)(h(v\otimes w))=\sum h_{(1)}f(v)\otimes h_{(2)}g(w)=h((f\otimes g)(v\otimes w))$. Both sides are linear and pure tensors span by [F4], so $f\otimes g$ is $H$-linear. The tensor maps preserve identities and compositions because their values agree on pure tensors.

Since $\varepsilon$ is a unital algebra map, $h\cdot c=\varepsilon(h)c$ satisfies $1_H\cdot c=c$ and $(ab)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)$; hence $k_\varepsilon$ is a left $H$-module by [F2]. The maps in [F5] are the proposed unit maps.

For $u\in U,v\in V,w\in W$, coassociativity writes the iterated coproduct in either parenthesization as $\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}\otimes h_{(3)}$. Both $\alpha(h\cdot((u\otimes v)\otimes w))$ and $h\cdot\alpha((u\otimes v)\otimes w)$ are therefore $\sum h_{(1)}u\otimes(h_{(2)}v\otimes h_{(3)}w)$ after applying the canonical associator; thus $\alpha$ is $H$-linear. For the left unit map, $\lambda(h\cdot(c\otimes v))=\sum\varepsilon(h_{(1)})c\,h_{(2)}v=c\,hv=h\cdot\lambda(c\otimes v)$ by the left counit identity. For the right unit map, $\rho(h\cdot(v\otimes c))=\sum h_{(1)}v\,\varepsilon(h_{(2)})c=h\cdot\rho(v\otimes c)$ by the right counit identity. Pure tensors span, so all three maps are $H$-linear on their full domains.

For the converse, use the regular left modules $H,H$. The action formula gives $b\cdot(1_H\otimes1_H)=\Delta(b)$ and $(ab)\cdot(1_H\otimes1_H)=\Delta(ab)$. By the assumed associativity of this tensor-module action, $\Delta(ab)=(ab)\cdot(1_H\otimes1_H)=a\cdot\bigl(b\cdot(1_H\otimes1_H)\bigr)=a\cdot\Delta(b)=\sum a_{(1)}b_{(1)}\otimes a_{(2)}b_{(2)}=\Delta(a)\Delta(b)$, where the last equality uses the tensor-product algebra multiplication [F3]. The assumed unital action law gives $1_H\otimes1_H=1_H\cdot(1_H\otimes1_H)=\Delta(1_H)$. Thus $\Delta$ is a unital algebra map.

The assumed unital $H$-module structure on $k_\varepsilon$ gives $\varepsilon(1_H)=1$ and $\varepsilon(ab)=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)$ directly from its unit and associativity laws [F2]. Hence $\varepsilon$ is a unital algebra map.

Apply $H$-linearity of the canonical associator to the three regular modules at $((1_H\otimes1_H)\otimes1_H)$. The action on this left-parenthesized unit tensor is $(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(h)$, and applying the associator sends it to $\alpha((\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(h))$ in $H\otimes(H\otimes H)$. On the right-parenthesized unit tensor, the action is $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta(h)$. Since the associator sends the unit tensor to the right-parenthesized unit tensor, its $H$-linearity gives $\alpha((\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(h))=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta(h)$, precisely coassociativity with the canonical associator [F6].

The naturality squares for $\alpha,\lambda,\rho$ commute on pure tensors because each composite applies the same module maps to the same entries; linearity extends equality to all tensors. By [F7], the underlying vector-space associator and unit maps satisfy the pentagon and triangle. Since every arrow in these diagrams is now $H$-linear, the same equalities hold in $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$. This proves the forward assertion.

Apply $H$-linearity of $\lambda:k_\varepsilon\otimes H\to H$ at $1\otimes1_H$: it gives $\sum\varepsilon(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}=h$. Apply $H$-linearity of $\rho:H\otimes k_\varepsilon\to H$ at $1_H\otimes1$: it gives $\sum h_{(1)}\varepsilon(h_{(2)})=h$. These are the two counit identities, so $\varepsilon$ is a counit. Steps 1.5–1.7 prove the other converse axioms.

Let $H$ be a bialgebra over a field $k$, let $S:H\to H$ be an antipode satisfying

$$\sum S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}=\varepsilon(h)1_H=\sum h_{(1)}S(h_{(2)}),$$

and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional left $H$-module. The algebraic dual $V^*$ is the vector space of linear functionals $V\to k$ from [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. Give it the candidate left $H$-action

$$ (h\cdot f)(v):=f(S(h)\cdot v). $$

Set $\operatorname{ev}:V^*\otimes V\to k$, $f\otimes v\mapsto f(v)$, and set $\operatorname{coev}:k\to V\otimes V^*$, $1\mapsto\sum_i e_i\otimes e^i$ for any finite basis $(e_i)$ and its dual basis $(e^i)$. The tensor in this formula is basis-independent by [[lem-hh-finite-tensor-duality-and-canonical-coevaluation]]. In this page's convention, “left dual” means these displayed orientations $V^*\otimes V\to k$ and $k\to V\otimes V^*$. Some sources use “right dual” for the same orientations; the formulas here fix the convention. The next theorem proves the candidate action and maps give a left dual, without assuming $S$ bijective.

For left $H$-modules $V,W$, give the algebraic tensor product $V\otimes_k W$ the candidate action

$$h\cdot(v\otimes w)=\sum h_{(1)}v\otimes h_{(2)}w,\qquad \Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.$$

The sums are finite algebraic tensor sums; the tensor product and scalar conventions are those of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. The candidate unit object is $k_\varepsilon=k$ with $h\cdot c=\varepsilon(h)c$. For morphisms $f:V\to V'$ and $g:W\to W'$, the candidate tensor morphism is the usual linear map $f\otimes g$ determined by $(f\otimes g)(v\otimes w)=f(v)\otimes g(w)$ through [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]].

These formulas specify the proposed tensor operations; [[thm-hh-bialgebra-module-tensor-coherence]] proves that they are module actions and that the canonical associator and unit maps are morphisms in $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces.

1. The bilinear map $V^*\times W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$, $(f,g)\mapsto[v\otimes w\mapsto f(v)g(w)]$, induces an isomorphism $V^*\otimes W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$. For ordered bases $(v_1,\dots,v_m)$ of $V$, $(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ of $W$ with dual bases $(v_i^*)$, $(w_j^*)$, the image of $v_i^*\otimes w_j^*$ is the dual basis vector of $v_i\otimes w_j$ in the product basis of $V\otimes W$.
2. For every ordered basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ the element $\sum_{i=1}^nv_i^*\otimes v_i\in V^*\otimes V$ is independent of the basis and corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V$ under the isomorphism $V^*\otimes V\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)$, $f\otimes v\mapsto[x\mapsto f(x)v]$ ([[thm-hom-from-a-finite-dimensional-space-as-a-tensor-product]]). Its image under $\sigma_{V^*,V}$ is the corresponding element $\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$ of $V\otimes V^*$.
3. The evaluation $\mathrm{ev}:V^*\otimes V\to k$, $f\otimes v\mapsto f(v)$, and the coevaluation $\mathrm{coev}:k\to V\otimes V^*$, $1\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$, are independent of the basis and satisfy $(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\mathrm{ev})\circ\alpha_{V,V^*,V}\circ(\mathrm{coev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_V)=\mathrm{id}_V$ and $(\mathrm{ev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V^*})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{V^*,V,V^*}\circ(\mathrm{id}_{V^*}\otimes\mathrm{coev})=\mathrm{id}_{V^*}$, the unit isomorphisms $k\otimes V\cong V$, $V\otimes k\cong V$ being understood.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, $N$ a left $R$-module, and

$$\tau:M\times N\longrightarrow M\otimes_RN,\qquad \tau(m,n)=m\otimes n.$$

The map $\tau$ is balanced ([[def-balanced-and-bilinear-maps]]). For every abelian group $A$ and every balanced map $b:M\times N\to A$, there is a unique group homomorphism

$$\overline b:M\otimes_RN\longrightarrow A$$

such that $\overline b(m\otimes n)=b(m,n)$ for all $m,n$. Consequently composition with $\tau$ is a bijection

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ab}}(M\otimes_RN,A)\cong\operatorname{Bal}_R(M,N;A).$$

derivations.claim: Give $H\otimes H$ its tensor-product coalgebra, $\Delta_{H\otimes H}(a\otimes b)=\sum(a_{(1)}\otimes b_{(1)})\otimes(a_{(2)}\otimes b_{(2)})$ and counit $\varepsilon\otimes\varepsilon$. The tensor universal property [F5] defines these maps from their bilinear formulas, and the coalgebra identities follow on pure tensors from those for $H$; pure tensors span. Thus convolution on $\operatorname{Hom}_k(H\otimes H,H)$, $(f*g)(z)=\sum f(z_{(1)})g(z_{(2)})$, is associative by coassociativity and associativity of multiplication, with unit $u(\varepsilon\otimes\varepsilon)$, where $u(c)=c1_H$. The pairings $P(a\otimes b)=S(ab)$ and $Q(a\otimes b)=S(b)S(a)$ are bilinear and hence define linear maps by [F5]. The antipode equations applied to $ab$ give $(P*m)(a\otimes b)=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1_H=(m*P)(a\otimes b)$, where $m(a\otimes b)=ab$. The same equations give $(Q*m)(a\otimes b)=\sum S(b_{(1)})S(a_{(1)})a_{(2)}b_{(2)}=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1_H$ and $(m*Q)(a\otimes b)=\sum a_{(1)}b_{(1)}S(b_{(2)})S(a_{(2)})=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1_H$. Hence $P$ and $Q$ are both two-sided convolution inverses of $m$; in any associative unital algebra a two-sided inverse is unique, so $S(ab)=S(b)S(a)$. Substituting $1_H$ into either antipode identity gives $S(1_H)=1_H$.

For $h,g\in H$, $v\in V$ and $f\in V^*$, $1_H\cdot f=f$ by $S(1_H)=1_H$, and $(h\cdot(g\cdot f))(v)=f(S(g)S(h)v)=f(S(hg)v)=((hg)\cdot f)(v)$ by step 1.1. The action is linear in each variable from linearity of $S$, the module action on $V$, and [F3]. Thus the candidate formula is a unital left $H$-module action.

For $h\in H$, $f\in V^*$ and $v\in V$, the tensor action and evaluation give $\operatorname{ev}(h\cdot(f\otimes v))=\sum (h_{(1)}\cdot f)(h_{(2)}v)=\sum f(S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}v)=\varepsilon(h)f(v)=h\cdot\operatorname{ev}(f\otimes v)$ by the left antipode identity. Linearity extends this equality from pure tensors to all of $V^*\otimes V$.

Fix a finite basis $(e_i)$ of $V$ and its dual basis $(e^i)$. Under the canonical isomorphism $V\otimes V^*\to\operatorname{End}_k(V)$, $x\otimes f\mapsto[y\mapsto f(y)x]$, the tensor $h\cdot\operatorname{coev}(1)=\sum_{(h),i}h_{(1)}e_i\otimes(h_{(2)}\cdot e^i)$ acts on $v$ as $\sum_{(h),i}e^i(S(h_{(2)})v)h_{(1)}e_i=\sum_{(h)}h_{(1)}S(h_{(2)})v=\varepsilon(h)v$ by the dual-basis identity and the right antipode identity. Therefore $h\cdot\operatorname{coev}(1)=\varepsilon(h)\operatorname{coev}(1)=\operatorname{coev}(h\cdot1)$, so coevaluation is $H$-linear.

For $v\in V$, the first triangle composite sends $v$ to $\sum_i e_i\,e^i(v)=v$. For $f\in V^*$, the second sends $f$ to $\sum_i f(e_i)e^i=f$. These are the two identities in [F4], so the triangle identities hold as maps of vector spaces and hence as maps in $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$, since evaluation and coevaluation are $H$-linear by steps 1.2 and 1.3.

If $V=0$, its basis is empty, the coevaluation sum is $0$, and both triangle identities are the identity of the zero space. If $V$ is infinite-dimensional, every tensor $\sum_{i=1}^r v_i\otimes f_i\in V\otimes V^*$ corresponds to an endomorphism with image in $\operatorname{span}(v_1,\ldots,v_r)$; the identity on $V$ has infinite-dimensional image, so it cannot be such a tensor. This explains why the finite-dimensional hypothesis is essential for the stated coevaluation. No choice principle is used: only a finite basis of the given finite-dimensional $V$ is used.

Let $H$ be a bialgebra over a field $k$ with antipode $S$, meaning a linear map satisfying

$$\sum S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}=\varepsilon(h)1_H=\sum h_{(1)}S(h_{(2)}).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional left $H$-module and give $V^*$ the candidate action and maps of [[def-hh-left-dual-of-a-finite-hopf-module]]. Then $S(ab)=S(b)S(a)$ and $S(1_H)=1_H$; the candidate action makes $V^*$ a left $H$-module; evaluation $V^*\otimes V\to k$ and coevaluation $k\to V\otimes V^*$ are $H$-linear; and the two triangle composites are identities. No bijectivity of $S$ is assumed.

Let $k$ be a field and let $H$ be a $k$-vector space with associative unital multiplication $m$, unit $1_H$, coassociative comultiplication $\Delta:H\to H\otimes_k H$, and counit $\varepsilon:H\to k$. Assume $\Delta$ and $\varepsilon$ are unital algebra maps; this is the bialgebra interface used on this page. A left $H$-module is a unital left module in the sense of [[def-left-and-right-modules]]: its action satisfies $1_Hv=v$ and $(hh')v=h(h'v)$. Let $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ be the category whose objects are all left $H$-modules and whose morphisms $f:V\to W$ are $k$-linear maps satisfying $f(hv)=h f(v)$ for every $h\in H$ and $v\in V$.

For left $H$-modules $V,W$, give the algebraic tensor product $V\otimes_k W$ the candidate action

$$h\cdot(v\otimes w)=\sum h_{(1)}v\otimes h_{(2)}w,\qquad \Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.$$

The sums are finite algebraic tensor sums; the tensor product and scalar conventions are those of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. The candidate unit object is $k_\varepsilon=k$ with $h\cdot c=\varepsilon(h)c$. For morphisms $f:V\to V'$ and $g:W\to W'$, the candidate tensor morphism is the usual linear map $f\otimes g$ determined by $(f\otimes g)(v\otimes w)=f(v)\otimes g(w)$ through [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]].

These formulas specify the proposed tensor operations; [[thm-hh-bialgebra-module-tensor-coherence]] proves that they are module actions and that the canonical associator and unit maps are morphisms in $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$.

Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces.

1. The bilinear map $V^*\times W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$, $(f,g)\mapsto[v\otimes w\mapsto f(v)g(w)]$, induces an isomorphism $V^*\otimes W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$. For ordered bases $(v_1,\dots,v_m)$ of $V$, $(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ of $W$ with dual bases $(v_i^*)$, $(w_j^*)$, the image of $v_i^*\otimes w_j^*$ is the dual basis vector of $v_i\otimes w_j$ in the product basis of $V\otimes W$.
2. For every ordered basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ the element $\sum_{i=1}^nv_i^*\otimes v_i\in V^*\otimes V$ is independent of the basis and corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V$ under the isomorphism $V^*\otimes V\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)$, $f\otimes v\mapsto[x\mapsto f(x)v]$ ([[thm-hom-from-a-finite-dimensional-space-as-a-tensor-product]]). Its image under $\sigma_{V^*,V}$ is the corresponding element $\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$ of $V\otimes V^*$.
3. The evaluation $\mathrm{ev}:V^*\otimes V\to k$, $f\otimes v\mapsto f(v)$, and the coevaluation $\mathrm{coev}:k\to V\otimes V^*$, $1\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$, are independent of the basis and satisfy $(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\mathrm{ev})\circ\alpha_{V,V^*,V}\circ(\mathrm{coev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_V)=\mathrm{id}_V$ and $(\mathrm{ev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V^*})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{V^*,V,V^*}\circ(\mathrm{id}_{V^*}\otimes\mathrm{coev})=\mathrm{id}_{V^*}$, the unit isomorphisms $k\otimes V\cong V$, $V\otimes k\cong V$ being understood.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, $N$ a left $R$-module, and

$$\tau:M\times N\longrightarrow M\otimes_RN,\qquad \tau(m,n)=m\otimes n.$$

The map $\tau$ is balanced ([[def-balanced-and-bilinear-maps]]). For every abelian group $A$ and every balanced map $b:M\times N\to A$, there is a unique group homomorphism

$$\overline b:M\otimes_RN\longrightarrow A$$

such that $\overline b(m\otimes n)=b(m,n)$ for all $m,n$. Consequently composition with $\tau$ is a bijection

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ab}}(M\otimes_RN,A)\cong\operatorname{Bal}_R(M,N;A).$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

derivations.claim: Since $S$ is antimultiplicative by [F1] and bijective by [A1], $S^{-1}$ is also antimultiplicative: applying $S$ to $S^{-1}(g)S^{-1}(h)$ gives $hg$, so injectivity gives $S^{-1}(hg)=S^{-1}(g)S^{-1}(h)$. Also $S^{-1}(1_H)=1_H$.

For $h\in H$, $f\in V^*$, $h\cdot j_V(v)(f)=j_V(v)(S(h)\cdot f)=(S(h)\cdot f)(v)=f(S^2(h)v)=j_V(S^2(h)v)(f)$. Thus the bidual formula holds. For finite-dimensional $V$, $j_V$ is a vector-space isomorphism by [F3], so it is $H$-linear exactly when $S^2(h)v=hv$ for all $h,v$. In particular $S^2=\mathrm{id}_H$ suffices for all finite-dimensional modules. If $H$ is finite-dimensional and this condition holds for every finite-dimensional module, apply it to the regular module $H$ and $v=1_H$ to get $S^2(h)=h$.

For $h,g\in H$, $v\in V$, and $f\in V^*$, $1_H\cdot f=f$ and $(h\cdot(g\cdot f))(v)=f(S^{-1}(g)S^{-1}(h)v)=f(S^{-1}(hg)v)=((hg)\cdot f)(v)$ by step 1.1. Linearity follows from linearity of $S^{-1}$, the action on $V$, and the algebraic dual operations [F5]. Thus $V^*$ is a left $H$-module.

Applying $S^{-1}$ to the two antipode equations in [A1], and using antimultiplicativity of $S^{-1}$ from step 1.1, yields $\sum S^{-1}(h_{(2)})h_{(1)}=\varepsilon(h)1_H$ and $\sum h_{(2)}S^{-1}(h_{(1)})=\varepsilon(h)1_H$.

If $f:V\to W$ is $H$-linear, then $f(pv)=pf(v)$, so $j_p$ is natural. Finally $p$ acts on $V\otimes W$ by $p\otimes p$ because it is group-like; therefore $j_{p,V\otimes W}(v\otimes w)$ corresponds to $j_{p,V}(v)\otimes j_{p,W}(w)$ under the canonical finite tensor-dual identification [F3]. Since $\varepsilon(p)=1$, the same compatibility holds on the unit object. Thus $j_p$ is monoidal.

For $v\in V$ and $f\in V^*$, $\widetilde{\operatorname{ev}}(h\cdot(v\otimes f))=\sum f(S^{-1}(h_{(2)})h_{(1)}v)=\varepsilon(h)f(v)=h\cdot\widetilde{\operatorname{ev}}(v\otimes f)$ by the first identity in step 2.2. The bilinear evaluation descends to $V\otimes V^*$ by [F4], so it is $H$-linear.

Let $\Theta:V^*\otimes V\to\operatorname{End}_k(V)$ send $f\otimes v$ to $[x\mapsto f(x)v]$. By [F3], $\sum_i e^i\otimes e_i$ corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V$. Hence $h\cdot\widetilde{\operatorname{coev}}(1)=\varepsilon(h)\widetilde{\operatorname{coev}}(1)=\widetilde{\operatorname{coev}}(h\cdot1)$; coevaluation is $H$-linear.
On $v\in V$, the first triangle composite gives $\sum_i e^i(v)e_i=v$; on $f\in V^*$, the second gives $\sum_i f(e_i)e^i=f$. These dual-basis expansions prove the two right-dual triangle identities.

If $V$ is one-dimensional, the dual-basis sums have one term and the same computations apply. Choosing a basis of the given finite-dimensional space uses no arbitrary-index choice. $$ (a+b)_n:=a_n+b_n,\qquad (ab)_n:=\sum_{i+j=n}a_i b_j. $$

The closure of these operations and the commutative-ring axioms are established by [[lem-polynomial-operations-preserve-finite-support]] and [[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]].

A **field** is a set $F$ equipped with two binary operations $+$ (addition) and
$\cdot$ (multiplication) and two distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$ of $F$,
satisfying:

- **(A)** $(F, +)$ is an abelian group with identity $0$: addition is
  associative and commutative, $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$, and every $x$ has an
  additive inverse $-x$ with $x + (-x) = 0$.
- **(M)** Multiplication is associative and commutative **on all of $F$**, and
  $x \cdot 1 = x$ for every $x \in F$; moreover $(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$ is an
  abelian group with identity $1$, so every $x \ne 0$ has a multiplicative inverse
  $x^{-1}$ with $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$.
- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

We write $x - y := x + (-y)$ and $x/y := x \cdot y^{-1}$ (for $y \ne 0$), and
abbreviate $x \cdot y$ as $xy$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

derivations.claim: The maps $\Delta$ and $\varepsilon$ are well-defined linear maps because every polynomial has a finite coefficient expansion [F1]. On monomials, $\Delta(t^m t^n)=t^{m+n}\otimes t^{m+n}=\Delta(t^m)\Delta(t^n)$ and $\varepsilon(t^m t^n)=1=\varepsilon(t^m)\varepsilon(t^n)$; the formulas also preserve $1$. Bilinearity extends multiplicativity to all polynomials.

If an antipode $S$ existed, its left convolution identity at $t$ would give $S(t)t=\varepsilon(t)1=1$. Every polynomial multiplied by $t$ has constant coefficient zero, while $1$ has nonzero constant coefficient by [F5]. This is impossible, so the bialgebra is not Hopf.

For each monomial $t^n$, $(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(t^n)=t^n\otimes t^n\otimes t^n=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta(t^n)$ and $(\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(t^n)=t^n=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\Delta(t^n)$. Since monomials span $k[t]$, these identities hold for all polynomials; together with step 1.1 they prove that $H$ is a bialgebra.

The actions $p(t)\cdot c:=p(0)c$ make $V=W=k$ unital left $H$-modules because evaluation at zero is a unital algebra map. On $1\otimes1\in V\otimes W$, $t$ acts by $\Delta(t)=t\otimes t$, hence by $0\otimes0=0$. The theorem [F4] makes the diagonal formula a module action on all of $V\otimes W$; it uses only the bialgebra structure proved in steps 1.1 and 2.1.

Thus the tensor module exists without an antipode. To check the example's claim about the underlying dual vector space, take $e=1\in V=k$ and $e^*(c)=c$, which spans $V^*$ by [F6]. Define $p(t)\cdot e^*=p(0)e^*$. For $p(t)=\sum_n a_nt^n$ and $q(t)=\sum_n b_nt^n$, the constant coefficient of $pq$ is $a_0b_0=p(0)q(0)$, and $1(0)=1$; hence this is a unital $H$-module action. It is not a left-dual object in $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$: $t$ acts by zero on $e^*\otimes e$ under the diagonal action, so evaluation sends $t\cdot(e^*\otimes e)$ to $0$, while $t\cdot\operatorname{ev}(e^*\otimes e)=t\cdot1=\varepsilon(t)1=1$. Since $0\ne1$ by [F5], evaluation is not $H$-linear.

A **group** is a monoid $(G,*,e)$ ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) in which every
element is invertible ([[def-invertible-element]]). Written out, a group is a set
$G$ with a binary operation $*$ ([[def-binary-operation]]) and an element
$e \in G$ such that

- **(G1)** $(x * y) * z = x * (y * z)$ for all $x, y, z \in G$;
- **(G2)** $e * x = x = x * e$ for every $x \in G$;
- **(G3)** for every $x \in G$ there is $y \in G$ with $y * x = e = x * y$.

By [[lem-identity-unique]] the element $e$ of (G2) is unique, and by
[[lem-inverse-unique]] the element $y$ of (G3) is unique for each $x$ and is
determined by either one of the two equations alone. So the notations $e$ for the
identity and $x^{-1}$ for the inverse of $x$ are legitimate, and asserting
$y * x = e$ alone already says $y = x^{-1}$.

A group is **abelian**, or **commutative**, when its operation is commutative:
$x * y = y * x$ for all $x, y \in G$.

**Notation.** The operation is usually written multiplicatively, $xy$ for
$x * y$, with identity $e$ (or $1$) and inverse $x^{-1}$. For an abelian group it
is often written additively, $x + y$, with identity $0$ and inverse $-x$; the two
notations describe the same notion and nothing below depends on the choice. We
write $G$ for the group when the operation is understood.

derivations.claim: The group algebra $H$ has basis $1,s$ and relation $s^2=1$. Define $\Delta(1)=1\otimes1$, $\Delta(s)=s\otimes s$, $\varepsilon(1)=\varepsilon(s)=1$, and $S(1)=1$, $S(s)=s$, extending linearly. Let $k$ be a field and let $H$ be a $k$-vector space with associative unital multiplication $m$, unit $1_H$, coassociative comultiplication $\Delta:H\to H\otimes_k H$, and counit $\varepsilon:H\to k$. Assume $\Delta$ and $\varepsilon$ are unital algebra maps; this is the bialgebra interface used on this page. A left $H$-module is a unital left module in the sense of [[def-left-and-right-modules]]: its action satisfies $1_Hv=v$ and $(hh')v=h(h'v)$. Let $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ be the category whose objects are all left $H$-modules and whose morphisms $f:V\to W$ are $k$-linear maps satisfying $f(hv)=h f(v)$ for every $h\in H$ and $v\in V$.

For left $H$-modules $V,W$, give the algebraic tensor product $V\otimes_k W$ the candidate action

$$h\cdot(v\otimes w)=\sum h_{(1)}v\otimes h_{(2)}w,\qquad \Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.$$

The sums are finite algebraic tensor sums; the tensor product and scalar conventions are those of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. The candidate unit object is $k_\varepsilon=k$ with $h\cdot c=\varepsilon(h)c$. For morphisms $f:V\to V'$ and $g:W\to W'$, the candidate tensor morphism is the usual linear map $f\otimes g$ determined by $(f\otimes g)(v\otimes w)=f(v)\otimes g(w)$ through [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]].

These formulas specify the proposed tensor operations; [[thm-hh-bialgebra-module-tensor-coherence]] proves that they are module actions and that the canonical associator and unit maps are morphisms in $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$.

Let $H$ be a bialgebra over a field $k$, let $S:H\to H$ be an antipode satisfying

$$\sum S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}=\varepsilon(h)1_H=\sum h_{(1)}S(h_{(2)}),$$

and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional left $H$-module. The algebraic dual $V^*$ is the vector space of linear functionals $V\to k$ from [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. Give it the candidate left $H$-action

$$ (h\cdot f)(v):=f(S(h)\cdot v). $$

Set $\operatorname{ev}:V^*\otimes V\to k$, $f\otimes v\mapsto f(v)$, and set $\operatorname{coev}:k\to V\otimes V^*$, $1\mapsto\sum_i e_i\otimes e^i$ for any finite basis $(e_i)$ and its dual basis $(e^i)$. The tensor in this formula is basis-independent by [[lem-hh-finite-tensor-duality-and-canonical-coevaluation]]. In this page's convention, “left dual” means these displayed orientations $V^*\otimes V\to k$ and $k\to V\otimes V^*$. Some sources use “right dual” for the same orientations; the formulas here fix the convention. The next theorem proves the candidate action and maps give a left dual, without assuming $S$ bijective.

Let $H$ be a bialgebra over a field $k$ with antipode $S$, meaning a linear map satisfying

$$\sum S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}=\varepsilon(h)1_H=\sum h_{(1)}S(h_{(2)}).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional left $H$-module and give $V^*$ the candidate action and maps of [[def-hh-left-dual-of-a-finite-hopf-module]]. Then $S(ab)=S(b)S(a)$ and $S(1_H)=1_H$; the candidate action makes $V^*$ a left $H$-module; evaluation $V^*\otimes V\to k$ and coevaluation $k\to V\otimes V^*$ are $H$-linear; and the two triangle composites are identities. No bijectivity of $S$ is assumed.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.
